Key points Newer GLDs significantly reduce the combined risk of seizure and epilepsy in older adults by 24% compared to placebo. GLP‐1 receptor agonists show the most promise for late‐onset seizure and epilepsy reduction. When analyzed separately, newer GLDs use was associated with a statistically significant reduction in late‐onset seizure, but not epilepsy, risk. The study highlights the need for further investigation into newer GLDs' anti‐epileptogenic effects. 1. INTRODUCTION Current anti‐seizure medications (ASMs) lack disease‐modifying or preventative, that is, anti‐epileptogenic, potential. 1 One of the primary challenges in anti‐epileptogenic drug discovery is the diverse etiology underlying epilepsy. Late‐onset epilepsy (LOE), typically starting after the age of 60–65 years of age, is one of the largest contributors to epilepsy burden, is an acquired form of epilepsy, making it a primary target for potentially anti‐epileptogenic drugs. 2 One of its most common etiologies is cerebrovascular disease, with diabetes mellitus (DM) being a common risk factor. 3 The newer glucose‐lowering drugs (GLDs), beyond their established effectiveness in managing diabetes, seem to have pleiotropic effects, including neuroprotection and anti‐inflammatory properties. A recent randomized controlled trial (RCT) shows that a newer GLD significantly slows Parkinson's disease, suggesting protection against neurodegeneration. 4 They may have anti‐neuroinflammatory properties as they show protective benefits against multiple sclerosis. 5 Etiopathogenesis of late‐onset epilepsy is thought to be a confluence of neurodegeneration and vascular damage, which raises the intriguing possibility that these drugs may potentially impact seizure and epilepsy development. 6 , 7 Therefore, we performed a meta‐analysis of RCTs of these drugs to investigate if newer GLDs have any protective benefit against seizure and epilepsy. 2. METHODS 2.1. Search strategy and study selection We conducted a comprehensive search of MEDLINE and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) from inception to April 2024 to identify RCTs that compared newer GLDs Dipeptidyl Peptidase‐4 [DPP‐4] inhibitors, Glucagon‐Like Peptide‐1 receptor agonists [GLP‐1RAs], and sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2 [SGLT2] inhibitors; details (Table S1 ) to placebo. Given that investigating the impact of a drug on seizure risk or epileptogenesis should have several months to years of follow‐up, we searched for studies on cardiovascular and renal outcomes. Additionally, adverse event reporting in these RCTs was more thorough and consistently included seizures and epilepsy. We also manually searched references from screened studies and relevant reviews to identify any other potential studies. The following MEDLINE search strategy was used: (Randomized Controlled Trial [MeSH Terms]) AND (newer glucose‐lowering drugs [MeSH Terms]) OR (SGLT2 inhibitors [MeSH Terms]) OR (DPP‐4 inhibitors [MeSH Terms]) OR (GLP‐1 agonists [MeSH Terms]) AND (cardiovascular [Title/Abstract]) OR (myocardial infarction [Title/Abstract]) OR (stroke [Title/Abstract]) OR (renal [Title/Abstract]) OR (kidney [Title/Abstract]) OR (albuminuria [Title/Abstract]). 2.2. Screening process Two independent reviewers used the following screening criteria: Inclusion criteria: (1) Randomized placebo‐controlled cardiovascular and renal outcome trials; (2) trials enrolled adults (≥18 years) with or without type 2 DM; and (3) trials reporting epilepsy or seizure adverse events. Exclusion Criteria: (1) Observational studies (e.g., cohort studies, case–control studies); (2) RCTs comparing different newer GLD classes; (3) Post hoc analyses; (4) Unregistered trials; and (5) Trials with unpublished/incomplete results on www.clinicaltrials.gov . 2.3. Data collection and extraction We used a standardized data extraction form to collect relevant information from eligible studies, including author information, publication date, trial ID, baseline participant characteristics, intervention details, follow‐up duration, outcome measures (cardiovascular or renal), and reported adverse events of seizure, and epilepsy. The latter, along with the number of strokes (ischemic and hemorrhagic), were extracted from trial results published on www.clinicaltrials.gov . We extracted information of incidence of strokes are the most common etiology underlying LOE and can potentially confound the effect of newer GLDs on seizure and epilepsy risk. 2 Adverse events reported as status epilepticus and convulsions were included as seizures. Epilepsy included all subtypes, regardless of whether it was unclassified or subclassified as generalized or focal. Seizures directly attributed to alcohol withdrawal were excluded from the analysis. Different dosages of newer GLDs within a single trial were combined. We assessed the quality of each included study using the Cochrane risk of bias assessment tool, Version 2. 8 2.4. Statistical analysis We used descriptive statistics to summarize the demographic characteristics of study participants. Frequency counts with percentages were used to present categorical data. Mean with standard deviation (SD) was used to demonstrate continuous variables. We employed the Mantel–Haenszel method to calculate pooled relative risk (RR), odds ratio (OR), and 95% confidence interval (CI) for the risk of the following events: seizure, epilepsy, combined seizure and epilepsy, and strokes. We performed a combined seizure and epilepsy risk analysis because of lack of information about the precise definitions used to classify seizure and epilepsy in the trials. For example, it is unclear from the available data if a first unprovoked (remote) seizure after a stroke was classified as only a seizure or, more appropriately, as epilepsy. In addition, subgroup analyses were conducted based on the class of newer GLDs (DPP‐4 inhibitors, GLP‐1RAs, and SGLT2 inhibitors). The chi‐squared ( χ 2 ) test assessed the study's heterogeneity and interaction between subgroups. Post hoc, after we found a low‐event rate for seizures and epilepsy, sensitivity analysis was performed using Peto's method to recalculate the OR. Peto's method is not recommended as a default meta‐analysis method. 9 However, it can be used when the events of interest are infrequent (<1%) and the studies have similar numbers in two comparator groups. 10 In the manuscript, we prioritized the Mantel–Haenszel method for our analysis due to its ability to control for confounding variables, its robustness to zero cells compared to Peto's method, and its ability to provide RR for a more straightforward interpretation of the association when analyzing rare events. 9 Potential publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot. Statistical significance was set at a two‐sided p ≤ 0.05. All statistical analyses were performed using RevMan. 11 3. RESULTS Out of 413 identified studies, 27 met the criteria for inclusion in the meta‐analysis. Figure S1 shows the PRISMA flowchart. The risk of bias was low for all domains except for selective reporting because seizures and epilepsy were not prespecified outcomes (Figure S2 ). No publication bias was detected (Figures S3–S6 ). There were five trials for DPP‐4 inhibitors, eight for GLP‐1Ras, and 14 for SGLT2 inhibitors. The meta‐analysis included 197 910 participants, with 52% in the newer GLD group and 48% in the placebo group. The average age of the patient population was 64.9 (SD 5.9) years, and 65.6% were males. The mean follow‐up duration averaged 29.2 months (SD 12.6). Seizures and epilepsy events were reported as adverse events in all the included studies. Table 1 details the study characteristics, participant demographics, intervention type, follow‐up duration, and seizure and epilepsy incidence in the drug and placebo groups. Seizure and epilepsy (combined outcome) A total of 182 (0.19%) patients in the placebo arm compared to 154 (0.015%) patients receiving newer GLDs had incident seizure or epilepsy during the follow‐up. The pooled meta‐analysis (Figure 1 ) found that people who received newer GLDs had a significantly lower risk of suffering seizures than the placebo group (RR: 0.76, 95% CI: 0.62–0.95, p = 0.01). The ORs calculated using Mantel–Haenszel and Peto's method showed similar association strength and statistical significance (Figures S11 and S12 , respectively). As noted in Figure 1 , among the newer GLD classes, the patients taking GLP‐1 receptor agonists had a statistically significant reduced seizure and epilepsy risk compared to placebo (RR = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.46–0.98; p : 0.034). FIGURE 1 Meta‐analysis of the effects of newer GLDs on seizure and epilepsy risk, combined, and subgrouped by the type of newer GLD (Mantel–Haenszel RR). 3.2. Seizures Seizures occurred in 126 (0.132%) placebo patients and 109 (0.105%) newer GLD patients. A total of two studies (Table 1 : study #5 and 24) in the drug arm and four studies (Table 1 : study # 9, 10, 27, and 26) in the placebo arm reported a single post‐stroke seizure or epilepsy event. The pooled meta‐analysis (Figure 2 ) found that people who received newer GLDs had a significantly lower risk of seizures than the placebo group (RR = 0.78, 95% CI: 0.60–1.00; p : 0.05). OR calculated using Mantel–Haenszel and Peto's method showed similar association strength and statistical significance (Figures S7 and S8 , respectively). No statistical heterogeneity was observed in the meta‐analyses (all p > 0.05). As noted in Figure 2 , among the newer GLD classes, the patients taking GLP‐1 receptor agonists had a statistically significant reduced seizure risk compared to placebo (RR = 0.60, 95% CI: 0.38–0.94; p : 0.03). FIGURE 2 (A) Meta‐analysis of the Effects of Newer GLDs on only Seizure Risk, subgrouped by the type of newer GLD (Mantel–Haenszel RR). (B) Meta‐analysis of the Effects of Newer GLDs on only Epilepsy Risk, subgrouped by the type of newer GLD (Mantel–Haenszel RR). 3.3. Epilepsy A total of 56 (0.059%) patients in the placebo arm were reported to have incident epilepsy during the follow‐up compared to 45 (0.044%) patients receiving newer GLDs. The pooled meta‐analysis (Figure 2B ) showed that patients taking newer GLDs had a lower risk of incident epilepsy compared to placebo (RR = 0.75, 95% CI: 0.51–1.11; p = 0.15), but this difference was not statistically significant. OR calculated using Mantel–Haenszel and Peto's method showed similar association strength and statistical significance (Figures S9 and S10 , respectively). No evidence of statistical heterogeneity was observed in the meta‐analyses (all p > 0.05). Subgroup analyses of the newer GLD classes did not reveal significant associations between their use and reduced epilepsy risk. 3.4. Stroke A total of 944 (0.99%) of patients in the placebo arm had strokes compared to 953 (0.93%) patients receiving newer GLDs. The pooled meta‐analysis showed no statistically significant difference in the stroke risk ratio in patients taking newer GLDs compared to placebo (RR = 0.94, 95% CI: 0.86–1.03; p = 0.21; Figure S13 ). The OR calculated using Mantel–Haenszel and Peto's method showed a similar lack of difference between the two groups (Figures S14 and S15 , respectively). 4. DISCUSSION Our meta‐analysis of 27 RCTs, which included almost 200 000 patients with a mean age of 65 years, reveals a potentially reduced risk of seizures and epilepsy when taking newer GLDs compared to placebo. During an average follow‐up of more 2 years, older adults taking newer GLDs had a 24% lower risk of seizures and epilepsy, combined, which was even higher in individuals taking GLP‐1 receptor agonists like Semaglutide (brand name Ozempic®). Independent analysis of seizures and epilepsy revealed significantly lower seizure, but not epilepsy, risk in patients taking newer GLDs. These findings align with preclinical studies, which show that all three newer GLD classes reduce seizure and epileptogenic activity in animal models. 12 , 13 , 14 Their putative anti‐epileptogenic mechanisms are multifactorial. DPP‐4 inhibitors, like sitagliptin, may work via an antioxidant effect, maintaining GABA levels and reducing neuroinflammation. 14 Similarly, liraglutide, a GLP‐1 receptor agonist, may protect against epilepsy by reducing chronic inflammation and mitochondrial stress. 15 Erdogan et al. posits a potential dual anti‐epileptogenic mechanism for SGLT2 inhibitors like dapagliflozin, whereby it restricts cerebral glucose availability to mitigate hyperexcitability and reduces sodium transport across neuronal membranes for a stabilizing effect. 16 In addition to basic science findings, there is sufficient clinical data to justify their investigation as anti‐LOE agents in humans. A complex interplay among cerebrovascular risk factors, stroke, and dementia leads to LOE. 6 , 7 Newer GLDs' have already demonstrated a pleiotropic effect beyond lowering glucose levels. They provide cerebrovascular protective benefits, reduce the risk of all‐cause dementia, significantly slow down neurodegeneration, and improve neuroinflammation. 5 , 17 , 18 , 19 Therefore, it seems likely that newer GLDs can target the intertwined pathophysiology underlying LOE, and their potential protection against late‐onset seizures and epilepsy may not be too surprising. However, the incidence of stroke does not explain the observed reduction in seizures and epilepsy in our meta‐analysis. Many of the newer GLDs, like GLP‐1 receptor agonists, have been hailed as “game‐changing” drugs, showing benefits in as varied diseases as alcohol use disorders and infertility. 20 , 21 , 22 It is critical to point out that newer GLDs' substantial protective benefit against late‐onset seizures and epilepsy, when analyzed independently, despite the abovementioned pathophysiological reasons, is statistically precarious with the former and falls short of reaching significance against the latter. This lack of strong statistical significance of seizures and epilepsy, individually, could be secondary to a major limitation of our study—seizure, and incident epilepsy were not the primary or secondary outcomes of the RCTs; instead, the information was extracted from the adverse effects reported on www.clinicaltrials.gov . The underreporting of seizures and incident epilepsy in either or both study arms can impact our findings. Conversely, there is possibly no anti‐epileptogenic benefit, or it is so tiny that a much larger sample size is needed to detect it with a higher statistical certainty. It is unclear whether the ILAE's practical definition of epilepsy, requiring either two unprovoked seizures or one unprovoked seizure with a remote brain insult, was used in reporting adverse events in the included RCTs. 23 To overcome this uncertainty, we decided to analyze the combined outcome of seizure and epilepsy. The longer follow‐up needed for diagnosing epilepsy after a first unprovoked seizure without a remote brain injury may explain the significant reduction in seizure risk, but not epilepsy, in our study. Alternatively, these drugs may only have a direct anti‐seizure effect but not an anti‐epileptogenic effect. Future studies that examine sustained seizure control after newer GLDs' discontinuation can help differentiate whether they have an anti‐seizure or anti‐epileptogenic mechanism because, in the latter case, there should remain a sustained seizure control after treatment cessation. Despite the average patient age being 65 years, some incident seizures and epilepsy cases may not have been late‐onset, as studies included adults over 18 years old. Due to inconsistent reporting of glucose‐lowering metrics in the included RCTs, we could not assess if the difference in seizure and epilepsy risk was associated with newer GLD's neuroprotective effects from glucose reduction. Also, despite a large sample size, the low seizure and epilepsy event rate poses some challenges to the precision of our estimates. However, post hoc, we performed Peto's method as a sensitivity analysis to counter this limitation, but the conclusions remained unchanged. Aside from a potentially direct anti‐epileptogenic effect of newer GLDs, our finding may be partly or entirely due to decreased comorbidities, like diabetes and obesity, that lead to or predispose to LOE. Nonetheless, our findings, in combination with preclinical studies, should encourage continued investigations into newer GLDs potential anti‐epileptogenic effects using varying methodologies and diverse, large population datasets, especially from specific older adult populations at significantly higher risk of epilepsy development like stroke patients. The included RCTs did not provide information to conduct such a specific subpopulation analysis. Additionally, unmeasured confounding factors with imbalanced randomization could influence the observed association. 5. CONCLUSION This meta‐analysis suggests that newer GLDs may have protective benefits against late‐onset seizures and epilepsy. Our findings are strengthened by supporting evidence of anti‐epileptogenic effects emerging from animal studies and the robust human data demonstrating their neuroprotective effects against cerebrovascular pathology, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation. Future research must validate and challenge our meta‐analysis findings, especially because LOE is a growing global challenge that is potentially amenable to preventative therapies. documents.title: Cenobamate add-on therapy for drug-resistant focal epilepsy.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Although most people with epilepsy achieve complete seizure cessation, approximately one-third of those with the condition continue experiencing seizures despite the use of antiseizure medications (ASMs) given as monotherapy or polytherapy. In this review, we summarised the evidence from randomised controlled trials (RCTs) about cenobamate as an add-on treatment for focal epilepsy uncontrolled by one or more concomitant ASMs.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the efficacy and tolerability of add-on oral cenobamate for the treatment of drug-resistant focal-onset seizures, defined as seizures persisting despite treatment with one or more ASMs.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web) and MEDLINE Ovid (September 2022). In addition, we contacted the manufacturer of cenobamate and experts in the field to enquire after any ongoing or unpublished studies.
SELECTION CRITERIA: RCTs comparing add-on cenobamate to placebo or another ASM in people with focal epilepsy uncontrolled by one or more concomitant ASMs.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: Two review authors independently selected trials for inclusion, extracted data, performed risk of bias assessment, and assessed the certainty of the evidence using the GRADE approach. Our primary outcomes were at least a 50% reduction in total seizure frequency, seizure freedom, and the occurrence of adverse events. We used an intention-to-treat approach for our primary analyses. For each outcome we estimated summary risk ratios (RRs) with their 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We summarised the estimates of effects and certainty of the evidence for each outcome in a summary of findings table.
MAIN RESULTS: We included two studies (659 adult participants, 442 allocated to cenobamate and 217 to placebo). The overall RR for at least a 50% reduction in seizure frequency for add-on cenobamate at any dose compared to placebo was 2.17 (52% versus 24%, 95% CI 1.66 to 2.84; 2 studies, 605 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). The RR for seizure freedom for add-on cenobamate at any dose compared to placebo was 4.45 (16% versus 5%, 95% CI 2.25 to 8.78; 2 studies, 605 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). The RR for the occurrence of adverse events for add-on cenobamate at any dose compared to placebo was 1.14 (77% versus 67%, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.27; 2 studies, 659 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). We judged the two included RCTs as at low or unclear risk of bias. Both studies were sponsored by the drug company that produces cenobamate.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Add-on cenobamate is probably better than placebo in reducing the frequency of seizures by at least 50% and in achieving seizure freedom in adults with focal epilepsy uncontrolled by one or more concomitant ASMs (moderate level of certainty). Its use is probably associated with an increased risk of adverse events (moderate level of certainty). Further prospective, controlled trials are required to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of add-on cenobamate compared to other ASMs. The efficacy and tolerability of cenobamate as adjunctive treatment for focal epilepsy in children should be further investigated. Finally, the long-term efficacy and tolerability of add-on cenobamate treatment in people with other epilepsy types (e.g. generalised epilepsy) or specific epilepsy syndromes, as well as its use as monotherapy, require additional study.

documents.title: Mortality in patients with epilepsy: a systematic review.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Epilepsy is linked to a significantly higher risk of death, yet public awareness remains low. This study aims to investigate mortality characteristics, to reduce epilepsy-related deaths and improve prevention strategies.
METHODS: This study systematically reviews mortality data in relevant literature from PubMed and Embase up until June 2024. Data quality is assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and analysis includes trends, regional differences, and the economic impact of premature death. Global Burden of Disease (GBD) data are used to validate trends. In addition, a review of guidelines and expert statements on sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) is included to explore intervention strategies and recommendations.
RESULTS: Annual mortality rates of epilepsy have gradually declined, mainly due to improvements in low-income countries, while high-income regions have experienced an upward trend. Male patients exhibit higher mortality rates than females. Age-based analysis shows that the elderly contributes most to this increase due to chronic conditions such as cardiovascular disease and pneumonia related to epilepsy. This may be a key factor contributing to the increased mortality among epilepsy patients in aging high-income regions. Accidents and suicides are more prevalent in low-income regions. The highest mortality risks occur in the early years post-diagnosis and during prolonged, uncontrolled epilepsy. SUDEP remains a leading cause of death.
CONCLUSION: This study highlights the impact of gender, region, and disease duration on epilepsy mortality. Future research should focus on elderly epilepsy patients mortality characteristics and personalized interventions for SUDEP.
documents.conclusions: This study highlights the impact of gender, region, and disease duration on epilepsy mortality. Future research should focus on elderly epilepsy patients mortality characteristics and personalized interventions for SUDEP.

Keywords: Epilepsy, Mortality, Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy (SUDEP), Global Burden of Disease (GBD) status released display-pdf yes is-in-collection-domain yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Received 2024 Dec 29; Revised 2025 Feb 26; Accepted 2025 Feb 28; Issue date 2025. Introduction Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder that affects over 65 million people globally, characterized by recurrent seizures [ 1 ]. According to the GBD study, approximately 140,000 individuals with idiopathic epilepsy died worldwide in 2021. A Swedish longitudinal cohort study found that people diagnosed with epilepsy face a 14-fold increase in all-cause mortality [ 2 ]. Despite these alarming statistics, public awareness of the mortality risks linked to epilepsy remains low, often leading to insufficient attention to this critical issue [ 3 ]. Deaths among epilepsy patients can be either directly linked to the epilepsy—such as SUDEP or status epilepticus—or indirectly related, involving accidents, drowning, or suicide. In addition, individuals with epilepsy are more likely than the general population to die from respiratory diseases, cancers, and vascular conditions, pointing to underlying causes that warrant deeper investigation [ 4 , 5 ]. Despite these known risks, the economic burden and precise causes of death within this population have not been thoroughly documented or analyzed. Presently, guidelines on SUDEP are sparse, and those that exist (e.g., ANN) are typically rated as offering “low” levels of evidence [ 6 ]. This highlights the critical need for high-quality evidence to guide the development of strategies aimed at reducing epilepsy-related mortality. Utilizing data from the GBD study and existing literature data, we will investigate mortality disparities within different subgroups, with a focus on risk profiles influenced by geographic, gender, and age-related factors. The study will assess both direct and indirect causes of death among epilepsy patients and evaluate existing guidelines, including those for SUDEP, to determine their quality and applicability. This study aims to better understand the mortality risks associated with epilepsy and identify key areas for prevention. By analyzing mortality patterns, economic impacts, and the effectiveness of current guidelines, we will provide recommendations to reduce premature deaths in epilepsy patients. Method Search strategy To obtain a comprehensive overview of overall mortality data for epilepsy, we searched PubMed and Embase for articles published in English from inception until June 2024. The search strategy for PubMed was ((“Epilepsy”[Mesh] OR EPILEPSY[Text Word]) AND (“Mortality”[Mesh] OR “mortality”[Subheading] OR MORTALITY[Text Word] OR “Death”[Mesh])). For Embase, the search terms were (epilep*) AND (‘mortality’ OR ‘death’ OR ‘Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy’ OR ‘SUDEP’). Inclusion and exclusion criteria Inclusion criteria were: Retrospective and prospective studies providing overall mortality data for epilepsy, including sample size and follow-up duration. Cross-sectional studies with clear follow-up duration with same type of data. Studies reporting the annual mortality or death numbers with the proportion of specific causes of death in the epilepsy population. Exclusion criteria were: Studies without the required data. Non-original articles (e.g., reviews, editorials, or commentaries). Studies where the mortality of the included population does not represent the overall regional population. Examples include studies exclusively focusing on specific subgroups such as pregnant women, children, or patients with status epilepticus, as such inclusion may introduce significant bias. Studies focusing on interventions for epilepsy using surgical procedures or neurostimulation techniques were not excluded under exclusion criteria 4 but were instead analyzed separately. Quality assessment and accuracy of data We assessed the quality of the included studies using a modified version of the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale and the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) epidemiological study standards, made by Musa M. Watila et al. Studies scoring below 4 out of a possible 9 points were excluded. Even after removing low-quality studies, we still identified substantial heterogeneity in the literature on epilepsy-related mortality. Some approaches employ inverse variance weighting and random-effects models to derive weighted average mortality rates [ 7 ]; however, high heterogeneity and limited variance data in primary studies complicate these analyses. To address these challenges, our methodology integrates the latest data from all eligible studies to establish specific reference values with a larger sample size. By excluding low-quality studies and incorporating a broader body of literature, we mitigate the impact of small sample sizes, thereby enhancing the reliability of our findings while minimizing bias. Data extraction Two researchers independently extracted the data, and any discrepancies were resolved by a third researcher. We extracted the following data: publication year, study type, follow-up duration, characteristics of the epilepsy population, sample sizes of male and female participants, number of deaths, standardized mortality ratio (SMR), region type (high-income, low-income, or rural areas), whether the patients included were newly diagnosed or had chronic conditions, provided or annual mortality, and proportions of specific causes of death. The classification of high-income and developing countries follows the United Nations Development Program (UNDP) classification based on the Human Development Index (HDI). Death data were sourced from national registries, follow-up records, death certificates, hospital records and health department records. Literature data analysis Python 3.11 (Python Software Foundation) and the Seaborn package were used for data analysis and visualization. The sample size-weighted annual mortality rate for all relevant studies was calculated using the formula: ∑ (number of deaths/follow-up duration)/∑ (epilepsy patient sample size). Standard Error (SE) = ∑ death number / ( follow - up duration ) 2 /∑ (epilepsy patient sample size). For each study, the calculated annual mortality was also presented as (number of deaths/follow-up duration)/(number of epilepsy patients). Mortality differences and the composition of causes of death were compared among various groups. In addition, temporal changes in subgroup mortality were analyzed based on study type, gender, regional characteristics, and features of the epilepsy population, using the formula: ∑ (number of deaths from a specific cause or total number of deaths)/∑ (epilepsy patient sample size). Scatter plots of mortality rates for each subgroup were generated to examine shifts in mortality risk over time, with the x-axis representing the median follow-up year. To explore the relationship between disease duration and mortality, simple linear regression models with breakpoints were fitted. Inflection points in the mortality curves were then identified using a likelihood ratio test. Global burden of disease (GBD) data analysis To validate the above analysis, we used the GBD database as the data source for analyzing epilepsy-related incidence and mortality. Data on the prevalence and mortality of epilepsy across various age groups, both globally and by country, were retrieved from the GBD database, covering the period from 1980 to 2021 to observe trends over time. The analysis included calculations of epilepsy incidence and mortality across different genders and age groups, with particular attention to trend changes in high-income countries. A linear regression model was employed to assess changes in mortality, providing 95% confidence intervals. Data analysis was primarily conducted using Python 3.11 and the Seaborn package. Literature review of guideline-like SUDEP publications This study also consolidates the current understanding of SUDEP, a leading cause of epilepsy-related mortality, and examines intervention strategies by reviewing recommendations, guidelines, expert consensus statements, and systematic reviews. Inclusion criteria focused on authoritative documents, such as clinical guidelines and expert statements, or systematic reviews that offer specific recommendations, while excluding original research, protocols, commentaries, and outdated documents. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across databases such as PubMed and Embase, as well as evidence-based medicine (EBM) platforms, including NICE, SIGN, TRIP, and Cochrane. After screening titles, abstracts, and full texts, duplicate and irrelevant entries were excluded to ensure that only the most current and relevant sources were analyzed. Data extraction focused on publication type, SUDEP risk factors, intervention recommendations, and the level of supporting evidence. Results Study selection 4538 articles were retrieved from PubMed and 7073 from Embase. After removing duplicates, 8817 articles remained. Following the screening of titles and abstracts, 8533 articles were excluded. Full-text reviews were conducted on the remaining 284 articles, of which 204 were subsequently excluded, leaving 80 studies on the general epilepsy population, 38 studies focusing on surgical interventions and 10 studies on neurostimulation (Fig. 1 ). Among these 80 studies, 23 were retrospective cohort studies, 34 were prospective cohort studies, and 23 were either database studies, cross-sectional studies, case–control studies, or other study designs [ 7 – 86 ]. Fig. 1 Study selection Of the included studies, 58 were conducted in high-income countries or regions, while 22 were from low-income countries or regions. Specifically, 23 studies were based on regional-level data from national registries, 25 were population- or community-based studies, and 37 were hospital-based investigations. We categorized all studies that provided data on the number of deaths, follow-up duration, and the number of epilepsy patients, or those that directly reported the annual mortality rate of epilepsy patients (Supplementary Table 1). Mortality characteristics In general epilepsy population, 67 studies, which provided data on subjects and deaths, with a total sample size of 741,378, showed an average annual mortality rate of 1.23% (95% CI: 1.22–1.24%), corresponding to 8922.38 deaths per year. Gender differences were observed, with male patients having a higher mortality rate (1.46%) compared to females (1.11%). Studies from low-income regions (21 studies, sample size of 21,172) showed a lower mortality rate of 0.99%, compared to 1.23% in high-income regions (46 studies, sample size of 720,206). This could be due to more accurate medical records and aging populations in high-income regions. In addition, rural studies (14 studies, sample size of 155,283) reported a higher mortality rate of 1.39%. Mortality rates also differed across study types, with hospital-based studies (36 studies) reporting a mortality rate of 1.22%, while population- or community-based studies (23 studies) had a lower rate of 0.93%, likely due to the inclusion of a broader range of epilepsy patients, including those with less severe forms of the condition. The general epilepsy population primarily received pharmacological treatment. To complement this, we additionally included studies focusing on surgical interventions and neurostimulation techniques. 38 studies met the inclusion criteria for postoperative outcomes, along with 10 studies on neurostimulation therapies. In both groups, males accounted for approximately 54% of the study populations, and the heterogeneity of the literature was high for both approaches. The overall annual mortality rate for surgical interventions was calculated as 0.56% (95% CI: 0.50–0.63%). Pediatric patients (< 18 years) had a lower postoperative annual mortality rate of 0.38%, while adult patients exhibited a higher rate of 0.76%. In the field of neurostimulation therapies, the overall annual mortality rate was 1.15% (95% CI: 1.27–1.35%). Specifically, the annual mortality rate for vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) was 1.23%, while that for responsive neurostimulation (RNS) was 0.69% (Fig. 2 ). Fig. 2 Comparative analysis of overall mortality rates calculated across different subgroups As shown in (Fig. 3 a, 12 studies focusing on the general population revealed varying trends. Except for two Brazilian studies (Gomes, Marleide da Mota; Ferreira), which showed a yearly decline, all other studies from high-income countries demonstrated an upward trend in mortality. Notably, three studies from Sweden, the UK, and the US reported particularly high mortality rates, which may be associated with the statistical methods employed by the respective national statistical authorities. Fig. 3 Analysis of mortality characteristics. A Literature review data analysis; B GBD data analysis. a Reported number of epilepsy-related deaths in the general population across 12 studies, with studies providing multi-year data shown as line plots. b Temporal trends in mortality rates as calculated from various studies. c Gender-specific mortality rate trends over time. d Comparison of mortality rate trends between high-income and low-income regions. e Mortality rate trends on surgery group and neurostimulation group over time. f Mortality and prevalence rates of idiopathic epilepsy across different income groups, based on Global Burden of Disease (GBD) data. g Age-specific mortality trends over time for the general population and high-income groups idiopathic epilepsy patients, based on GBD data. h Trends in all-cause mortality and idiopathic epilepsy mortality for populations over 70 years old in high-income regions, based on GBD data In the year-mortality scatter plot (Fig. 3 b, 3c), we observed heterogeneity across studies. While the overall data from the literature suggested a slight upward trend in mortality, the GBD data indicated a slight decline. This discrepancy could be due to the fact that most studies are from high-income countries with larger sample sizes, which may obscure the global situation. A consistent pattern, however, is that both epilepsy mortality and prevalence are rising in high-income regions, while the opposite trend is observed in low-income countries (Fig. 3 d, 3f). Over time, the mortality in both the surgical and neurostimulation groups have shown a consistent downward trend (Fig. 3 e). GBD data on age-specific mortality in high-income countries reveals that compared to the global scenario (Fig. 3 g), there has been a sharp increase in deaths among epilepsy patients aged 50 and above, especially in those over 75 years old, while changes in younger age groups are less pronounced. For patients aged 50–74, the number of epilepsy-related deaths increased by an average of 100.91 individuals per year [95% CI: (90.21, 111.62)]. In the 75 + age group, deaths rose by an average of 182.01 individuals per year [95% CI: (163.20, 200.83)], indicating that the rising mortality among epilepsy patients in high-income countries is largely driven by older age groups. When comparing the mortality of the general elderly population and elderly epilepsy patients in high-income countries (Fig. 3 h), mortality among elderly epilepsy patients has significantly increased, whereas mortality in the general elderly population has gradually decreased. This contrast suggests that the rise in epilepsy-related mortality in high-income countries is not solely due to population aging. Epilepsy itself plays a substantial role in the increasing mortality among the elderly. We will discuss the cause-of-death analysis in more detail later. Cause of death analysis For general epilepsy population, a total of 45 studies provided data on causes of death, summarized in Supplementary Table 2. The aggregated results (Fig. 4 ) indicate that epilepsy-related deaths, including SUDEP and status epilepticus (SE), account for 16.29% of total deaths. Among these, SUDEP accounts for 2.9%, while deaths due to SE account for 1.86%. Notably, the relatively low proportion of SUDEP may be attributed to inconsistent definitions across studies. The boundaries between SUDEP, epilepsy-related deaths, and deaths from unknown causes are sometimes blurred, leading to the misclassification of some SUDEP cases as general epilepsy-related deaths [ 88 ]. Accidents and suicides together account for 7.89% of deaths, with suicides contributing 2.42%. Tumor-related mortality is responsible for 16.35% of all deaths, with brain tumors contributing 5.51% and other tumor types accounting for 14.67%. Cardiovascular diseases account for 15.26%, while cerebrovascular diseases account for 14.4%. Pneumonia and respiratory diseases make up 8.24% of the total mortality. In conclusion, epilepsy-related factors and tumors are the leading causes of death, followed by vascular diseases. Despite the relatively low incidence of SUDEP, epilepsy-related deaths remain a major contributor to mortality. This may reflect the difficulty in accurately categorizing SUDEP and other epilepsy-related deaths. Fig. 4 Comparison of causes of death. A Comparison of data from all studies. B Comparison of causes of death between high-income and low-income regions In high-income regions, tumor-related deaths are much higher than that in low-income regions (16.39 vs. 9.93%), and mortality from cardiovascular diseases is also significantly higher (15.34 vs. 7.76%). On the other hand, in low-income regions, accidents and suicides account for a much larger proportion of deaths (40.75 vs. 7.65%), with drowning alone contributing 17.26%. Epilepsy-related mortality is slightly higher in low-income regions compared to high-income regions (17.72 vs. 16.29%). Overall, while high-income regions experience higher mortality from tumors and cardiovascular diseases, low-income regions face a greater burden from accidents, suicides, and drowning. Changes in mortality risk of epilepsy with disease duration Among the 80 studies, 16 included patients with newly diagnosed epilepsy, while 6 focused on those with chronic epilepsy (Fig. 5 A). Newly diagnosed epilepsy refers to patients who have been diagnosed within the past 0–3 years, representing a relatively short disease duration during the study period. Chronic epilepsy, on the other hand, generally refers to patients diagnosed at least 4 years prior and still experiencing seizures. Our findings indicate that the mortality rate among newly diagnosed epilepsy patients is considerably higher than that of chronic patients. This disparity may be partly attributed to the fact that patients with severe epilepsy are more likely to die within the first few years following diagnosis. The total sample size for newly diagnosed epilepsy patients was 166,792, with an average annual mortality rate of 1.97%, compared to 9226 for chronic epilepsy patients, whose average annual mortality rate was 0.61%. There was significant variation in the annual mortality of newly diagnosed epilepsy across different regions and studies. Excluding a Korean study, which comprised 83% of the total sample size, the recalculated annual mortality for newly diagnosed epilepsy increased to 4.57%. Fig. 5 Comparison of mortality characteristics between newly diagnosed epilepsy and chronic epilepsy. A Comparison of overall mortality rates between newly diagnosed epilepsy and chronic epilepsy. B Trends in mortality risk after epilepsy diagnosis, compiled from eight studies. C Proportions of different causes of death in the newly diagnosed group and chronic epilepsy group All studies showed a marked decline in SMR during the first 3 years of disease duration. We identified the 2.5-year mark as a significant inflection point, prior to this point, mortality decreased rapidly at an average rate of 2.58% per year, while after this point, the decline slowed considerably to 0.28% per year ( p < 0.001). Furthermore, around 7–8 years post-diagnosis, a slight increase in SMR was observed. While three out of the eight studies support this trend, it has not yet reached statistical significance ( p = 0.137) (Fig. 5 B). Cause-of-death analyses between newly diagnosed (shorter disease duration) and chronic epilepsy (longer disease duration) groups revealed that patients with shorter disease durations had a higher proportion of SUDEP (19.77 vs. 17.39%), cerebrovascular disease (17.9 vs. 11.76%), and tumors (22.92 vs. 13.37%). (Fig. 5 C) These findings suggest that the higher mortality in newly diagnosed epilepsy patients may primarily result from two factors: the critical underlying causes of symptomatic epilepsy and the high risk of SUDEP during the early stages, when the condition is not yet fully controlled. In contrast, while the proportion of SUDEP remains high in chronic epilepsy patients, they experience significantly higher rates of accidents or suicides compared to newly diagnosed patients (16.91 vs. 9.72%). This suggests that psychological and safety-related risks tend to accumulate over time in chronic epilepsy, contributing to the more than threefold increase in suicide rates. In addition, chronic epilepsy patients show elevated mortality from pneumonia and respiratory diseases (14.21 vs. 5.78%) and cardiovascular diseases (13.37 vs. 6.12%), which we will explore in greater detail later. Review of SUDEP guidelines Despite the significant role of SUDEP in epilepsy-related fatalities, both physicians and patients often have limited awareness of the condition, as well as insufficient strategies for prevention and emergency response. This may be due, in part, to the currently unclear mechanisms underlying SUDEP. Our review found that there is a limited number of clinical guidelines addressing SUDEP, and the quality of evidence in these guidelines is generally low, highlighting a need for further research and clearer recommendation [ 89 ]. An analysis of 10 available guideline documents identified the main risk factors for SUDEP, including frequent generalized tonic–clonic seizures (especially when unmonitored at night), poor medication adherence, frequent changes in antiepileptic medications, long-term epilepsy history, cognitive impairments, young male gender, living alone, and structural brain abnormalities [ 90 – 99 ] (Supplementary Table 3). Poor seizure control is often associated with non-adherence to medication. In children, the primary risk factors include developmental delay, cognitive impairments, unmonitored nocturnal seizures, and long disease duration, although the incidence of SUDEP in children is only one-fifth of that in adults. The SUDEP incidence rate in adults is approximately five times higher than in children [ 89 ]. Currently, there are only three types of intervention and prevention strategies for SUDEP: informing patients and families about the potential for SUDEP, following guidelines to effectively control seizures, and using monitoring devices, particularly nocturnal monitoring systems. However, there is a lack of evidence supporting the effectiveness of these interventions. We identified only one comprehensive review that discussed emergency interventions for SUDEP, which include early oxygen administration, airway management, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). Discussion Through a comprehensive literature review, we identified substantial heterogeneity in studies on epilepsy-related mortality. Existing systematic reviews often summarize findings without calculating average mortality rates due to variations in study quality, follow-up duration, and sample sizes, making direct averaging inappropriate. As a result, many rely on a limited number of studies when reporting mortality rates and causes of death across different populations. Our methodology tackles the issue of high heterogeneity across studies by integrating the latest data from all eligible sources to derive more robust reference values. Through the exclusion of low-quality studies and the inclusion of a wider body of literature, we reduce the influence of small sample sizes, ultimately improving the reliability of our findings and minimizing bias. Overall, the annual mortality has gradually decreased, primarily due to the progress made in low-income countries. In contrast, high-income regions have seen a rising mortality trend. Furthermore, a clear gender disparity exists, with male patients demonstrating a higher mortality than their female counterparts. Age-based analysis indicates that this increase is primarily driven by the elderly population, who are more likely to experience chronic diseases related to epilepsy, such as cardiovascular disease and pneumonia. In contrast, the incidence of accidents and suicides is significantly higher in low-income regions. Disease duration analysis shows that the highest mortality risks occur in the early years following diagnosis and during prolonged, uncontrolled epilepsy. Regardless of region, gender, or disease duration, SUDEP remains one of the leading causes of death. Our results indicate that the mortality for drug-resistant epilepsy decreased by about half after surgery, which is similar to the findings of the systematic review by Sylvain Rheims et al. in 2022 [ 100 ]. However, some studies may have overlooked non-surgery-related deaths, and patient selection bias could also lead to an underestimation of the overall mortality rate. Jianwei Shi et al. (2024) found that RNS was more effective than VNS in controlling seizures [ 101 ]. Similarly, our findings suggest that RNS may be linked to a reduction in mortality, though further research is needed to validate this observation. The annual mortality for male epilepsy patients is 1.46%, significantly higher than the 1.11% for females, with the number of male patients being 1.09 times higher than females. This phenomenon may be attributed to various mechanisms, such as the neuroprotective effects of progesterone against seizures, stronger white matter connectivity between cortical regions in males, and the influence of androgens on GABA activity through reduced DNA methylation [ 102 – 105 ]. Men are also more likely to work in high-risk occupations, increasing their chances of head injuries. Lifestyle factors, such as alcohol consumption and smoking, may worsen epilepsy severity, and men are less likely to seek timely medical care, which may increase their risk of disease progression and death [ 105 – 111 ]. However, it is important to note that epilepsy in women can affect fertility, contributing to a significant global economic burden, which also warrants attention [ 112 ]. For the pregnant population, a meta-analysis has indicated that the mortality rate for women with epilepsy during pregnancy is approximately 10 times higher than that of the general pregnant population [ 113 ], According to an ongoing retrospective study by our research group, the annual mortality rate for pregnant women with epilepsy is around 0.1–0.13%. However, complications such as miscarriage and congenital abnormalities in offspring are more complex to address. As for adolescent epilepsy patients, this study did not perform a specific analysis. Generally, except for epilepsy in neonates, the incidence of sudden death in childhood epilepsy tends to be relatively low [ 92 , 114 ], and the mortality rate from status epilepticus is significantly lower than in adults [ 115 ]. Counterintuitively, the annual mortality in developed regions has gradually surpassed that in less developed regions. In high-income regions, deaths in epilepsy patients are more often linked to comorbidities such as tumors, cardiovascular diseases, and respiratory diseases, particularly in the elderly. This result aligns with the findings mentioned in the WHO Global Status Report on Noncommunicable Diseases, which highlights the increasing burden of chronic diseases in high-income countries. However, there is a lack of research on the causes of death in epilepsy patients across different age groups. Brain tumors can directly induce epilepsy, while other tumors may increase seizure risk through brain metastasis, paraneoplastic syndromes, or the effects of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) [ 116 ]. The GBD study provides mortality data exclusively for idiopathic epilepsy without specifying causes of death but offers valuable temporal and spatial insights. Our research builds on this by synthesizing the latest evidence on epilepsy-related mortality, identifying specific causes of death, and examining factors driving mortality trends and potential interventions. Previous reviews indicate that epilepsy-related mortality risk is significantly higher in high-income countries. This disparity is often attributed to incomplete or absent death registries in lower income areas. However, by mapping mortality trends across studies and integrating GBD data, we found the consistent downward trend in epilepsy-related mortality in low- and middle-income regions, as well as the contrasting mortality trends between elderly epilepsy patients and their non-epilepsy counterparts in high-income regions. These findings suggest that this difference may not primarily stem from registration errors. Instead, in aging high-income regions, epilepsy may exacerbate comorbidities, contributing to higher mortality among elderly patients. Analysis of causes of death indicates that in high-income regions, the primary causes of epilepsy-related mortality include respiratory and circulatory diseases, which are common comorbidities among elderly epilepsy patients. Based on these findings, we propose the hypothesis that the elevated epilepsy-related mortality in high-income regions may be linked to elderly epilepsy patients. The mortality in this population is not only associated with the inherently high risk of SUDEP but may also be related to long-term epilepsy-induced damage to the respiratory and cardiovascular systems. This could explain the increasing mortality rates among elderly epilepsy patients and the high proportion of deaths attributed to pneumonia and cardiovascular causes. Pneumonia is a leading cause of death, and often aspiration during seizures when patients lose consciousness, have a weakened gag reflex, or vomit leads to the inhalation of stomach contents or oral secretions. The risk of aspiration pneumonia increases with higher seizure frequency and longer disease duration, especially in patients with generalized seizures or status epilepticus (SE), potentially leading to death. Epilepsy may also cause neurogenic pulmonary edema, worsening the condition and increasing mortality risk [ 117 ]. Cardiovascular disease is another major contributor to the higher mortality in epilepsy patients in high-income countries. Repeated seizures may lead to structural changes in the heart, a condition known as “epileptic heart,” which is linked to SUDEP [ 118 ]. Abnormal brain electrical activity during seizures can induce arrhythmias or cardiac arrest, potentially causing myocardial injury through mechanisms involving catecholamines, leading to myocardial fibrosis and atherosclerosis. Studies have shown that epilepsy patients often exhibit reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), indicating systolic dysfunction, with diastolic function also being affected [ 119 ]. AEDs and vagus nerve stimulation may also have negative effects on the heart. According to Lende’s study, sinus tachycardia occurs in up to 80% of the seizures, while cardiac arrest is more common in focal epilepsy, with post-seizure cardiac arrest associated with SUDEP. Other abnormalities such as bradycardia, atrioventricular block, and ventricular fibrillation are occasionally observed [ 120 ]. Genetic mutations such as KCNQ1 and SCN5A may affect the function of both the heart and brain via ion channels, increasing the risk of cardiac complications in epilepsy patients [ 121 ]. High-risk patients, such as elderly epilepsy patients with comorbid cardiovascular diseases, should undergo continuous electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring, using devices such as implantable loop recorders (ILR) to monitor for arrhythmias. In low-income regions, accidents and suicides account for up to 40.75% of deaths. In some areas, such as the western Sichuan Basin in China, drowning constitutes more than 50% of deaths among epilepsy patients. These figures highlight the urgent need for better epilepsy education, awareness, and policy development in developing countries, especially to help patients avoid hazardous environments or workplaces. They also reflect the widespread safety risks and lack of emergency resources in low-income areas, highlighting the need for tailored safety measures, such as epilepsy detection devices. Moreover, seizure warning model could reduce the accidents of patients with epilepsy in daily life, which emphasized on the construction and application of wearable or convenient warning method. Currently, aside from standard practices such as controlling seizures and informing patients and their families about the risks of SUDEP, the use of monitoring devices is one of the few specific interventions. However, the ANN guidelines only provide a Class C recommendation for such devices due to a lack of sufficient evidence. Most population-based long-term follow-up studies indicate that the risk of death is highest within the first few years following diagnosis, with mortality decreasing in subsequent years. This may be due to a concentration of deaths in the early stages of severe epilepsy. On the other hand, newly diagnosed epilepsy patients often experience frequent, uncontrolled seizures. The high mortality during this period could be partly attributed to the lack of appropriate treatment and insufficient understanding of their condition [ 122 , 123 ]. SE in newly diagnosed epilepsy patients is a significant factor contributing to mortality. Studies have shown that approximately 23% of new epilepsy cases progress to SE [ 124 ], while other studies report this rate to be as high as 30%, with SE-related mortality ranging from 4.6 to 39% [121\p]. Another systematic review found that short-term mortality in elderly SE patients can reach 22–38%, while a large case series on new onset refractory status epilepticus (NORSE) reported a mortality of 23%. Timely diagnosis and treatment are critical in reducing mortality, as early can effectively reduce SE and its associated complications [ 121 ]. Although SE did not account for a very large proportion of deaths in our results, this does not imply that the mortality of SE is low. Besides, certain causes of epilepsy, such as brain tumors and cerebrovascular disease, as well as uncontrolled seizures, can lead to higher early mortality [ 122 ]. Over time, with appropriate treatment, most epilepsy patient’s conditions can be better controlled, leading to a reduction in mortality. As a result, chronic epilepsy patients often face a lower risk of death due to disease stabilization [ 122 ], which aligns with our findings. However, chronic epilepsy patients often face social stigma and discrimination. This stigma, arising from societal misunderstandings or internalized by patients, can lead to negative self-perceptions. It may also deter patients from seeking timely care and support, worsening their psychological burden and safety risks. This could explain the higher rates of suicide and accidents among chronic epilepsy patients, emphasizing the need for psychological interventions and social education [ 124 ]. Furthermore, chronic epilepsy patients experience a significant increase in mortality from causes such as cardiovascular disease and pneumonia. These factors may also explain the increase in mortality observed in some studies after 7 years of diagnosis. Regardless of any classification, SUDEP remains one of the most common causes of death. In the overall data, epilepsy-related causes account for the highest proportion of deaths, at 16.3%. Although SUDEP’s proportion in the overall assessment may not seem high, many papers suggest that the epilepsy-related deaths mentioned primarily refer to SUDEP [ 123 ]. SUDEP events often occur without witnesses, particularly at night or during sleep, when post-seizure terminal central apnea occurs, followed by cardiac arrest. Cardiac arrest and respiratory apnea in SUDEP are typically caused by brainstem dysfunction and autonomic nervous system dysregulation, which impair normal respiratory and cardiac control. In addition, serotonin system dysfunction and other neuromodulators such as adenosine and GABA may further suppress respiration and increase the risk of cardiac arrest. Some studies have also suggested that SUDEP may be caused by myocardial ischemia or ventricular fibrillation due to cardiac repolarization abnormalities triggered by seizures [ 118 ]. Although SUDEP emergency interventions are relatively simple (e.g., oxygen administration, airway management, cardiopulmonary resuscitation), the lack of access to equipment and insufficient training of emergency personnel often results in missed opportunities for timely intervention [ 124 ]. Therefore, it is crucial to develop portable and efficient emergency devices while strengthening the training of emergency responders to ensure they can competently operate these devices and respond quickly. Table 1 Key causes of death and key prevention Key target group Main causes of death Comments Epilepsy patients within 2.5 years of the first seizure Underlying causes, status epilepticus (SE) Treat underlying causes, earlier intervention, control seizures Epilepsy patients with a long disease duration (usually > 7 years); elderly chronic patients Cardiac and pulmonary comorbidities, suicide, or accidents Monitor comorbidities, emphasize psychological support, safety education, and protection Patients with long-term uncontrolled epilepsy; patients with uncontrolled generalized tonic–clonic seizures SUDEP Control seizures, prepare for cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) Patients with frequent nocturnal seizures and without monitoring SUDEP Control seizures, provide nocturnal monitoring devices, prepare for CPR Patients with high-risk heart gene mutation SUDEP, sudden cardiac death Control seizures, undergo ECG monitoring, prepare for CPR Patients in high-income countries Cardiac and pulmonary comorbidities, SUDEP Focus on comorbidities, increase awareness of SUDEP Patients in low-income countries SE, SUDEP, suicide, accidents Strengthen education and awareness, improve healthcare services, prioritize seizure control Epilepsy patients in rural areas Strengthen education, healthcare development, etc Male patients in the above groups require extra attention Avoid high-risk occupations, quit unhealthy habits, enhance safety and psychological education Limitations First, due to the broad time span of the included literature, the calculated annual mortality and causes of death distributions may not fully reflect the current situation. Second, the heterogeneity of the included studies is relatively high, including sample sources, study method, follow-up durations, and SUDEP definition standards. Third, detailed data on the causes of death across different age groups are scarce in the included studies. Summary In conclusion, there is an urgent need for more high-quality studies to strengthen clinical monitoring and SUDEP intervention strategies. First, research should address the rising mortality and changing causes of death in high-income countries, particularly in elderly epilepsy patients with comorbidities such as cardiovascular, cerebrovascular diseases, and cancer. Second, the high rates of epilepsy-related accidents and suicides in low-income regions point to gaps in patient management and persistent stigma. Lastly, improving the management of newly diagnosed epilepsy patients is crucial for better outcomes. Supplementary Information Below is the link to the electronic supplementary material. documents.title: Carbetocin versus oxytocin in prevention of postpartum hemorrhage after cesarean delivery in high-risk women. A systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To assess the value of carbetocin in prevention of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) after Cesarean delivery (CD).
SEARCH STRATEGY: Screening of PubMed, Web Of Science, Scopus, register clinical trials registry and Google scholar from inception to December 2023. The keywords used included postpartum hemorrhage, intraoperative blood loss, postoperative blood loss, Cesarean delivery and their MeSH terms.
SELECTION CRITERIA: All RCTs that compared carbetocin to oxytocin in women undergoing CD with risk factor for PPH. Fourteen studies including 3068 participants. Thirteen were written in English and one in Polish.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: The extracted data included location of the trial, number of centers involved in recruitment, the number of participants and their characteristics, details of the study groups and dose time and route of intervention and its comparator, primary and secondary outcome parameters and trial registration number and timing in relation to patients recruitment. The evaluated outcomes parameters included intraoperative and 1st 24 h post-operative blood loss, PPH, the hemoglobin changes after the procedure, the need for any additional uterotonic agents, surgical interventions or blood transfusion and drugs side effects.
MAIN RESULTS: Blood loss during the 1st 24 h after CD was evaluated in 11 studies with 2497 participants and revealed a mean difference (MD) of -111.07 with 95% CI of [-189.34 and -32.80 (P = 0.005, I2 97%). The hemoglobin changes after the operation was evaluated in 8 studies with 1646 participants and revealed a MD of -0.46 with 95% CI of -0.14 and -0.79 (P = 0.03, I2 96%). The incidence of PPH > 500 ml was reported in 8 studies with 1787 participants and revealed an Odd Ratio (OR) of 0.52 with 95%CI of [0.36, 0.77] (P 2 0%). The need for additional uterotonic agents was evaluated in 12 studies with 2663 participants and revealed an OR of 0.17 with 95% CI of 0.07 and 0.37 (P 2 88%). The need for blood transfusion was evaluated in 10 studies with 2439 participants and revealed an OR of 0.27 with 95% CI of 0.12 and 0.57 (P 2 20%). The need for additional interventions was evaluated in 3 studies with 1311 participants and revealed an OR of 0.67 with 95% CI of 0.28 and 1.60 (P = 0.37, I2 59%).
CONCLUSION: Carbetocin decreased the blood loss during the 1st 24 h after CD, post-operative hemoglobin drop, PPH the need for additional uterotonic agents and blood transfusion when compared to oxytocin.

Introduction A million Cesarean deliveries (CDs) or more are carried on yearly in the United States being the most common surgical there [ 1 ]. World health organization reported an incidence of CD of 15% [ 2 ]. Although the rate of CD is increasing in both developed and developing countries, yet the incidence vary largely among different low income countries with a rate of 52% in Egypt and less than 5% in Somalia [ 3 ]. CD provides a lower risk of maternal pelvic floor and neonatal birth injuries but carries a higher maternal surgical risk during the current and future pregnancies and a higher risk for development of neonatal respiratory distress [ 4 ]. The maternal morbidity during CD is double that occurs during vaginal delivery [ 5 ] with higher rates of hemorrhage, infections, anesthetic, thromboembolic complications, and even death [ 6 ]. Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) occurs in more than 14 million women and accounts for 70 000 maternal deaths yearly [ 7 ]. It is defined as more than 500 and 1000-mL blood loss during or within 24 h of VD and CD respectively [ 8 ]. Its risk is highest among low and middle income populations and the majority of maternal deaths in these countries are related to bleeding events as these counties lack the availability of high standard medical care [ 9 ]. The use of different uterotonic agents is recommended by WHO to prevent PPH in all deliveries [ 10 ]. The intravenous slow administration of 5 IU oxytocin is recommended by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists after fetal extraction to ensure adequate contractions giving the advantages of rapid placental delivery and reduction of intraoperative and postpartum blood loss [ 11 ]. Oxytocin has many disadvantages. Its half life is short (4–10 min) so intravenous infusion is needed to achieve a prolonged action which necessitates continuous medical observation [ 12 ]. The other disadvantage is the requirement of a special storage and transport system with a 2–8 °C. This is particularly important in limited resource areas especially in countries with hot and humid environments [ 13 ]. In 1997, an oxytocin analog with heat stability that binds oxytocin receptors and results in prolonged uterine contractions were developed. Carbetocin starts its action within 2 min and its action is maintained for 1 h after administration. The uterine contractions induced by carbetocin is one and half times more strong than that caused by oxytocin. Carbetocin presents an excellent alternative to the traditional oxytocin in less developed areas with limited storage and transport facilities [ 14 ]. Objective To compare the safety and efficacy of carbetocin and oxytocin in prevention of PPH after CD in high-risk women. Methods The PRISMA guidelines of randomized controlled studies (RCTs) were followed in this systematic review. It was registered with CRD42023492407 number. Eligibility criteria, information sources, search strategy The search databases included PubMed, Web Of Science, Scopus, register clinical trials registry and Google scholar from inception to December 2023. The key words used included carbetocin, postpartum hemorrhage, Intraoperative blood loss, Postoperative blood loss, Cesarean delivery and their MeSH terms. All related clinical trials and reviews reference lists were checked for possible study inclusions. Study selection Study selection based on PICO format. Population included women underwent CD with high risk for development of postpartum hemorrhage. Intervention women received carbetocin injection. Comparator: studies comparing carbetocin to oxytocin alone or when combined with another uterotonic drugs as misoprostol. Outcomes: blood loss. Types of included studies: only RCTs without any language limitations. Cohort, case control studies, case series, reviews and editorial opinion were excluded. All doses and routes of administration of both oxytocin and carbetocin were included. The database search, assessment of all articles and evaluation for inclusion or exclusion from the review were done by two authors independently. Any disagreement between them was discussed with other authors. After selection of the included studies, the data were extracted by two authors independently and any needed clarifications were obtained by contacting the corresponding author and other co-authors. The extracted data included location of the trial, number of centers involved in recruitment, the number of participants and their characteristics, details of the study groups and dose time and route of intervention and its comparator, primary and secondary outcome parameters and trial registration number and timing in relation to patients recruitment. The evaluated outcomes parameters included intraoperative and 1st 24 h post-operative blood loss, PPH, the hemoglobin changes after the procedure, the need for any additional uterotonic agents, surgical interventions or blood transfusion and drugs side effects. The Cochrane Handbook of Systematic Reviews recommendation for evaluation of RCTs were followed. Evaluated items included the generation of random sequence, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and outcome assessors, incomplete and selective data reporting beside the evaluation of other biases. The quality of evidence was evaluated using GRADE analysis which. Two authors (SA and WSR) assessed the quality of the individual studies following recommendations that include the number of the studies, their risk of bias, outcome inconsistency, indirectness of data, sample size and width of CI and publication bias. Statistical analysis The mean differences and OR and their 95% confidence interval (CI) were used to calculate the effect estimate of continuous and dichotomous data, respectively. The fixed or random effect was used according to studies heterogeneity. The heterogeneity was evaluated through assessed by Cochran’s Q test and I 2 statistic and a significant hetero1geneity was considered when I 2 statistic reached more than 40%. A significant effect was considered when the P value was below 0.05. All statistical calculations were done using the Review Manager (RevMan) version 5.4.1 (The Nordic Cochrane Centre, Cochrane Collaboration, 2020, Copenhagen, Denmark). Results Study selection, study characteristics The PRISMA flow chart describing the search results is shown in Fig. 1 Fig. 1 PRISMA flow chart Fourteen studies including 3068 participants (1519 subjected to carbetocin and 1398 subjected to oxytocin, 151 were subjected to B Lynch technique) were included in our meta-analysis [ 15 – 28 ]. Thirteen were published in English and one in Polish language [ 23 ]. All the studies were 2 arm except Mohamed et al. [ 25 ] was 3 arm study. Carbetocin was compared to oxytocin alone in one studies and compared to combined oxytocin and misoprostol in one study [ 20 ]. CD in the included studies was elective in seven studies, emergency in two studies and a mixture of both elective and emergency in five studies. CD were conducted under spinal anesthesia in six studies, under general anesthesia in two studies while in six studies the type of anesthesia was not specified. The dose of oxytocin was 5 IU in 1 study [ 16 ], 10 IU in 4 studies [ 17 , 22 , 23 , 28 ], 20 IU in five studies [ 19 – 21 , 25 , 26 ], 30 IU in three studies [ 18 , 24 , 27 ] and 40IU in one study [ 15 ]. The risk factor for PPH was specified as hypertensive disorder in three studies [ 15 , 16 , 22 ], Twin pregnancy in one study [ 21 ], obesity in one study [ 19 ] and general non-specified risk factor in nine studies. Eleven studies were conducted in a single center and three studies were conducted in two centers [ 19 , 25 , 27 ]. Seven studies were conducted in Egypt, 2 were conducted in Italy, one study in each of the following countries Bangladesh, China, Iran, Poland and Thailand. Among the included studies only five trials were prospectively registered. The characteristics of the included studies are presented in Table 1 . [0.15, 0.75] 0.008 3% Emergency 2 400 0.03 [0.00, 0.50] 0.01 NA Both 1 120 0.36 [0.11, 1.21] 0.10 NA Discussion This meta-analysis confirmed that the amount of blood loss during the first 24 h after CD, the post-operative hemoglobin drop, the occurrence of PPH, the need for additional uterotonic agents and blood transfusion were significantly lower in women who received carbetocin during CD compared to women treated with oxytocin. The need for additional intervention was not significantly different between the two groups of women. While women received oxytocin experienced more headache than women who received carbetocin, all other adverse effects named nausea, vomiting, fever, abdominal pain and hypotension showed non statistical significant differences between the two groups. The beneficial effect of carbetocin on blood loss was more evident in women who received 20 IU of oxytocin, under spinal and non-specified anesthesia, with twin pregnancy, obesity and general risk factors for PPH and in both elective and emergency CD. The improvement in hemoglobin drop was evident in women who received 30 and 40 IU of oxytocin, with twin pregnancy, hypertension, obesity and general risk factors for PPH and in both elective and emergency CD. The lower need for additional uterotonic agents were evident in all doses of oxytocin under all types of anesthesia with any risk factors and in both elective and emergency CD. These advantages of carbetocin over oxytocin could be related to its prolonged half-life allowing prolonged more efficient uterine contractility and subsequent decrease in blood loss and other outcome parameters. The half-life of carbetocin was reported as 40 min compared to only 1–6 min half-life of oxytocin [ 10 ]. Another explanation may be related to the difficult suitable storage and transport environment for oxytocin in countries with limited resources. On evaluation of oxytocin samples in limited resource countries, 45.6% of the studied samples failed to pass the quality tests [ 13 ]. Strengths and limitations Our meta-analysis provides the premier available proof of the safety and efficacy of carbetocin compared to oxytocin in improving uterine contractions after CD with the subsequent decrease in post-operative blood loss, PPH, the need for additional uterotonic agents and the needs for blood transfusion without a significant increase in drug adverse effects. We included all the available published RCTs without any language limitations. Complete and careful data extraction, assessment of the risk of bias and full analysis (both quantitative and qualitative) was done for all included studies. Extensive subgroup analysis was done for all the reported outcomes for all variables including the dose of oxytocin, type of CD, type of anesthesia used and the risk factors for PPH. We also carefully assessed the quality of evidence for all outcomes. The heterogeneity of the included studies regarding participants’ characteristics, doses and routes of oxytocin was the main limitation of our review. Not all articles reported the same outcomes. The location of research conduction was a mix of both developing and developed countries. Most of the studies were not prospectively registered. We tried to overcome these limitations through extensive subgroup analysis and performing the analysis using the random effect model. Comparison with existing reviews A previous systematic review conducted by Wen and colleagues [ 29 ] in 2020. They included 17 RCT that used carbetocin during both VD and CD. There was no subgroup analysis or assessment for the quality of evidence. Both Sun et al. [ 30 ] and Kalafat et al. [ 31 ] conducted a meta-analysis to compare carbetocin to oxytocin and included 24 and 30 studies, respectively. The included studies were a mix of benefits in both VD and CD. Both reviews lack subgroups analysis and assessment of quality of evidence. Beside this Kalafat review did not analyze the adverse effects of the drugs used. Onwochei and colleagues [ 32 ] focused on women undergwent Cd but their trial included only 5 RCTs and this small number did not allow for any subgroup analysis. A recent review by Jaffar and colleagues [ 33 ] included 46 trials. As it was a network meta-analysis, they compared carbetocin to various uterotonic agents not only oxytocin. Conclusion This systematic review concluded that the use of carbetocin during CD is associated with less blood loss during 1st 24 h after the operation (high evidence), reduced the incidence of PPH (high evidence), the hemoglobin drop (moderate evidence), the need for additional uterotonic agents (high evidence), and blood transfusion (high evidence) when compared to oxytocin without increase in adverse effects. We strongly recommend the use of carbetocin as a routine uterotonic agent in limited resource countries with unavailable storage and transport facilities to reach the goal of WHO of reducing maternal mortality based on its heat stable character. However being more expensive that oxytocin, individual cost effective assessment should be carried in each area guided by its resources to reach the decision of routine use or its use in high-risk women only.
